Two Bodies, One Story

Burst Monitor · the read from the Friday, October 23 close

Two Bodies, One Story

For three months the S&P 500's biggest shared move has not been up or down. It has been long the rest of the market, short the AI complex. Measured as the first principal direction of the field's returns, that long-short factor has been the market's dominant axis for 77 sessions — the longest such run on a 26-year record, by four times. This week the long side began to tighten into one block, the short side stayed at its trough, and Friday was the first day both fell together. The story count is falling because the two camps are the story. Whether they become one body is the question the next sessions answer.

Where we left off · two editions, one fork

Tuesday, Oct 13
The Crest Travels. The index had made a record on October 6 without its typical stock; then five shared crests traveled from the AI-hardware leaders to the utilities and railroads. Rotation, measured. The fork: it continues, or the field swings together on the way down.
Sunday, Oct 18
The Sorting. The index lost 2% while its median stock gained 2.6% — the sixth-widest week between them since 2000. Two groups held their membership and went opposite ways: an AI-hardware core down 7%, a financials-and-industrials block up 1%. The ten largest companies rolled down their cycles together; the field crested behind them. Seven things to watch.
This morning
Sol read first and then followed Jason's walk of the board — the story count falling toward its line, the shared storm cast, the agreement days, the hot edge of the spectrogram, the split dial, the map's float, the river's continuity. Jason's reframing of the story count — "a tale of two groups, with one having less freedom than the other" — became the measurement this edition is built on. Six of the seven watches answered; the table is in chapter 6.

1 · The tape

Week three of the rotation, and one common day

The index gave back half a percent. Its typical stock gained 1.4%. For the third week running, the stocks that rallied were the ones outside the AI trade and the stocks that fell were inside it — and then on Friday, for the first time in the episode, 365 of 501 names fell together.

Hold the two camps fixed by name and the week is simple. The 315 names the dial placed just past their crest on Tuesday — call them the crest 315, the long side of the rotation — gained 2.1% at the median with 79% up. The 115 it placed just past their trough — the trough 115: Nvidia, Meta, Alphabet, Broadcom, Micron and the names that trade with them — lost 1.9% with a third up. The ten largest companies, which are 39% of the index, lost 1.2% at the median: Meta −9.4%, Alphabet −6.0%, Broadcom −2.2%, Nvidia −1.5%; Apple +1.2% and Tesla +4.9% on the other side. The index's −0.47% is the cap-weighted net of those two sentences.

The two camps since August 13

median of each group's return since Aug 13, with the S&P 500 and the median of all 501 · gold ticks = closure days from Sep 28 (a shared crest, defined in chapter 5)

The gap opened after the record. On October 6, with the index at its high, the crest 315 and the trough 115 were within a point of each other since August 13 (−5.6% and −4.7% at the median); by Friday they were fifteen points apart, +1.7% against −13.9%, with the index at −2.3% and the median stock at −2.8% between them. The ten largest companies, −6.4% at the median since August, are what the index's weight is carrying. That is what a rotation looks like when the names are held fixed instead of re-sorted into winners and losers each week.

The week, day by day

Thursday and Friday were two different markets. Thursday (index −1.21%) was the loudest two-sided day of the episode: 338 of 501 names rose while the trough 115 lost 2.2% at the median and the ten largest 3.7% — Meta's print landed on the short side and the long side kept going. Friday (−0.52%) was the first common day: 365 names down, the crest 315 −0.9%, the trough −0.7%, the financials-and-industrials block −0.7%. Energy was the exception (+2.8% at the median, 18 of 21 up — Sol's count), cyclicals and staples the deepest losers. One common day inside three weeks of sorting; it matters because of what it does to the readers in the next two chapters, and it is not in those readers yet.

2 · The factor

The market's first direction is a pair trade

Jason's first observation on the board was the story count falling toward its crater line. The story count is the number of independent bets the market is pricing, and a falling count usually reads as the market becoming one body. Decomposed, this one is not. The biggest shared direction in the field's returns is not "the market up and down." It is long the crest, short the trough — and it has been for 77 sessions.

The story count, which the board also draws as degrees of freedom, is the effective number of independent directions in the ~500 stocks' standardized returns over a window — 21 sessions for the fast reader, 63 for the slow one. Twenty would mean twenty separate stories; three would mean a market moving on three. Historically the count collapses into a crater — below 55% of its trailing-year median — when one direction takes over: 2008, 2011, 2015, 2018, 2020, 2022, the spring of 2025. The fast reader fell from 11.9 to 8.5 this week and crossed the drawn line; the slow reader fell from 18.4 to 16.0 and sits far above it.

A count is one number summarizing a spectrum. Take the spectrum apart and two things decide what the count means. The first mode's share is how much of the field's variance rides on its single biggest direction. The same-sign share is what fraction of the 500 sit on the same side of that direction. In a normal tape the first mode is the market factor and the same-sign share is 99%: the median since 2000, with the tenth percentile at 94%. When the same-sign share drops to 80%, the biggest direction is a long-short factor — a pair trade at index scale — with a fifth of the names on the short leg.

The first mode over the last year, 63-session window

left axis: share of variance in the first mode (ink) and the second (gold) · right axis: the first mode's same-sign share (teal) · dashed = the record's medians · shaded = the split run, from July 8

Over the last 63 sessions the first mode carries 19% of the variance — the 10th percentile of the record — and the second mode 11%, the 96th. And the first mode's same-sign share is 79%: the 1st percentile. Loaded against the fixed camps, the first direction has the crest 315 on one side (89% of them positive) and the trough 115 off it entirely (48% positive — uncorrelated with it) with the AI-hardware 54 on the far side (37%). The second direction is a cyclicals-and-semis against defensives-and-energy axis: Emerson, United, Ametek, Goldman, Caterpillar, Morgan Stanley on one end; Exxon, Chevron, Conoco, Dow, Altria, Philip Morris on the other. Neither is the market.

runs of a two-sided first mode (same-sign share below 85%, 63-session window)sessionslowindex, next quarter from the lowworst drawdownstory-count crater within a quarter

The current run began on July 8 — the window that first contained the spring's AI-led rally alongside the start of the rotation — and reached its low of 74% same-sign on August 3. (The share has been under 85% on all but two sessions since June 24; the two exceptions sat at 85.1%. Read the run as 'since late June' with the threshold stated.) The record has four prior clusters of this shape, and they do not agree: the dot-com unwind of 2000–01 (old economy against new, the index down 7–13% over the following quarter without a crater, because the field was already as fragmented as it ever gets); December 2017, which the February 2018 crater followed; January 2020, which COVID followed; February 2021, the growth-to-value rotation, benign. Four cases is a list. What is not in dispute is the length: none of them lasted three weeks, and this one is in its sixteenth.

The fast reader against the line, last 45 sessions

PR21 (ink), PR63 (gold) and the 63-derived crater line (dashed)

What moved it: the 21-session first mode

its share of variance (ink, left) and its same-sign share (teal, right)

Here is the week's mechanism. The whole of the fast reader's fall is the 21-session first mode swelling — from 19% of the variance on October 16 to 28% on October 23 — while its same-sign share fell, from 86% to 78%. A direction that grows while becoming more two-sided is the pair trade getting louder, not the market unifying. And the construction says which day did it: the point labeled October 23 uses returns through October 22, so the last step is Thursday's split day — the trough 115 down 2.2% and the ten down 3.7% while 338 names rose. Friday's common day, the one that would push the same-sign share back toward one, enters on Monday's print.

What a crater looks like on the way in

Every one of the fifteen story-count craters on the record arrived with a whole first mode: same-sign share between 97% and 100%, carrying 26–54% of the variance. The common mode had taken over. Forty-two sessions before the onset the picture was more varied — the common mode's share ran from 11% to 36% — and the February 2018 crater started from almost exactly today's shape: same-sign 83%, share 11%, which became 99% and 33% by the onset forty sessions later. So a split, weak first mode can become a crater's common mode inside two months, and the path runs through the same-sign share climbing back toward one while the first mode grows. Today the first mode is growing with the same-sign share falling. That is the opposite of the crater path at this step. It is a reading of one week, not a projection.

3 · The long side

Which body lost its freedom

"A tale of two groups, with one having less freedom than the other." Run the story count inside each camp instead of across the field and the tale has a measurement: the short side has had less freedom all month, and this week the long side lost a third of its own in five sessions.

Freedom here is the same participation ratio, computed inside one group and divided by the most it could be — the window length or the group's size, whichever is smaller — so that a 315-name group and a 115-name group can be read on one scale. One means every name is its own story; near zero means the group moves as a block.

Freedom inside each camp, 21-session window

participation ratio as a share of its ceiling · the crest 315 (gold), the trough 115 (blue), the AI-hardware 54 (red), the financials-and-industrials 64 (teal)

The trough 115 have been at 0.31–0.39 since the start of October, and the AI-hardware 54 at their core at 0.22–0.31 — the tightest object on the board, with 42% of its variance in a single direction over the last 21 sessions. The AI complex has moved as a block all month. The crest 315 were the free group. They stood at 0.57 on October 5, at 0.50 on October 16, and at 0.34 on October 23: a third of their freedom gone in five sessions, landing almost on the trough's level. Their first mode's share went from 23% to 32%. The receivers of the rotation started moving as one block, and the field's story count fell because of it — not because the 115 did anything new.

Two qualifications the numbers insist on. First, at the quarter scale neither camp is unusually tight: each group's within-group first mode, over 63 sessions, sits at the 20th–30th percentile of its own history (a lookback — the casts were selected on Tuesday). The two bodies are each only ordinarily cohesive over the quarter; what sits at the first percentile is their opposition. The contraction is a short-horizon event so far. Second, the trough is a block in phase more than in returns: its own first mode at 21 sessions is only 70% same-sign this week — Thursday split the AI complex internally even as the dial reads it as one tight cluster. The dial measures where a stock is in its swing; the story count measures how its daily returns co-vary. The AI complex passes the first more cleanly than the second.

The story count fell because the long side tightened. The short side has been a block all month.

4 · The casts

Two hands, half a cycle apart

Hold the camps fixed and ask the dial where each one stands. The crest 315 share one position, just past their crest. The trough 115 share one position, just past their trough. The market as a whole has barely any position at all, because the two cancel.

The dial's hand is a group's average position in the cycle, and its R is how tightly the group agrees on it: 1.0 means every name at the same point, below 0.35 means no shared position worth reading. Held fixed since Tuesday, the crest 315 read R 0.89 at 0.15 of a cycle (just past home, descending) and the trough 115 R 0.81 at 0.65 (just past the trough). Half a cycle apart, both still coherent after a week in which both fell. The whole market's count hand is 0.37 — barely over the line — and its cap-weighted hand 0.17, a zero: the largest names are on both flanks.

The ten. A week ago the ten largest companies shared a tight hand (R 0.73) at 0.40, descending toward their trough, four of them already there. Now five sit at the trough — Nvidia, Meta, both Alphabet lines, Broadcom, Micron — Apple and Tesla are at home, and Microsoft and Amazon crossed from home into the descending quarter on Thursday. Their hand loosened to R 0.50 at 0.52. The AI names reached the trough the record said they would; the two that had held at home have started down. The other 491: R 0.39 at 0.13 — the swing branch's marker from last week, the rest locking through 0.55 while the ten descend, did not print.

The river: the groups kept their members while the field sorted

The river is the board's clustering of the 500 by who has moved in phase with whom over the last 63 sessions; its rooms are the clusters and the matched-J is how much each room's membership survived from one day to the next. Friday's matched-J was 0.81 — the 89th percentile of the 45-session window (Sol's count), with the last five days averaging 0.78 against 0.65 for the five before. The financials-and-industrials block that had split 42 / 8 / 1 on Thursday reunited to 48 / 2 / 1 on Friday: all eight separated names came back. The rooms are holding while the story count falls, and those are not two facts. Stable groups moving as blocks is a low story count with a two-sided first mode. The river and the story count are reading one geometry.

One caution the block itself supplies: the 64's phase hand went from R 0.50 to a zero over the same two days, and its narrow home-window occupancy ran 8 → 10 → 11 → 22 → 10 with only four of Thursday's 22 still there Friday. Membership reunited, phase alignment weakened, prices fell. Keep all three visible; none cancels the others.

5 · The floor

Who is holding the pressure

The map's week was a release and a float: six shared crests in a row, Thursday's the broadest of the episode, and then a Friday with no new impulse. The names holding the pressure are the long side of the rotation — 170 of the 186 below the floor are the crest 315.

A closure is a session on which at least 8% of the pool — 51 of 648 — crest together: a shared top in their own swings. The ledger prints six in a row, October 15 through 22, with Thursday's at 214 names: a third of the pool at home on the day the index lost 1.2%. That is the crest 315 cresting, seen from the pressure side, and it is one session behind the edge, where the record says the count prints high and settles. Friday's own tick is 40, quiet — the newest tick prints low (it fires on 11% of mornings as printed, 55% once revised), so Friday may yet become a closure on Tuesday's build. If it does, the question is whose: a closure whose closers are the trough cast would be the rotation's cast reversing for the first time.

The closure ledger, Sep 28 → Oct 23

Jason's point about the map's motion, from watching it rather than the still: the field is not draining toward the crowd. Measured, the newest step is a near-vertical float (R 0.96 at +83°, 498 of 501 names up); the printed five-session compass still points down (−71°) because it contains the release dives. Sideways, the average coupling to the market's pulse moved from −0.049 to −0.034 over two weeks and the names in the tightly-coupled crowd went from 24 to 26. Pressure refilled on the long side, and it is floating, and it has not recoupled. (Sol's decomposition; the per-name decay is exactly 2−1/21 to fourteen decimals.)

6 · The books

What the record says about the crossing

Three places the record can be asked. What followed the fast reader crossing its line while the slow reader stayed high. What the agreement book is printing, and when it printed it. And what last week's seven watches did.

The fast reader's crossing

The condition was written after seeing Friday's shape, so this is a lean with counts, not a probability. Since 2001 the fast reader has crossed under the slow reader's crater line, from above, while the slow reader stayed above it, 46 times with a full quarter of outcome behind each (Friday's is the 47th, pending). A slow-reader crater followed within a quarter in 37% of them, against 17% at base — twice the base — and the slow reader fell a median 0.9 over the quarter against −0.2. But the index ran better than base: +2.5% at the median over the next month (74% up) against +1.3%. The crossing has been a structure event more than a price event. Narrow it to today's shape — the slow reader still high (at least 1.5× its line; today 1.8×) and the index within 5% of its high (today −2.5%) — and the record has thirteen cases: no crater within a month, a crater within a quarter in 15% (base 17%), the index +2.4% over the next month with 85% up, and the quarter's tenth-percentile worst drawdown −12% against −15% at base (worst drawdown: the largest peak-to-trough fall inside the next 63 sessions). The one recent crossing that did crater, March 17 of 2025, came with the index already 7.6% below its high. The record's discriminator is whether the tape is already in a drawdown at the crossing — not the crossing itself.

The agreement book, and when it agreed

The amplitude book asks a different question of the same 500 stocks: not where each is in its swing but how loud it is — the size of its swing against its own history — and whether the names agree about that, across memory lengths from a month to three years. Rust on the spectrogram is agreement, blue is disagreement; an agreement day (a zero) is a session when the spread across names falls under its own trailing-year floor. Jason saw the recent prints: agreement days firing at several depths and a lot of rust in the last two weeks of the field.

Two things keep the trend honest. The mornings did not print these agreements. The saved first prints of October 14, 15, 19, 20 and 21 all read apart; the zeros are recognized in today's reconstruction, because every stock's loudness is recomputed when a day is added. They inform the approach without becoming "the instrument said so then." And the ruler's newest print is pegged at the other end: 15 of 16 memory rungs at their disagreement extreme, the one-year spread 1.48 against a 1.10 floor. "Crushed," in the book's vocabulary, means agreement; what Jason saw at the tail is a thin quiet tail — 2.8% of names at their own quiet extreme, the 27th percentile of its history, under a 5.3% loud tail. An asymmetry between the tails, not the crush end, and not a steady drain this week (Sol: last five days 3.4% against 3.1% for the five before).

The memory

The board's headline correlation, 0.90, is the strength of the relationship between the market's participation energy and its drawdown at the memory the instrument selects — 396 sessions, with energy lagging the drawdown by 168 sessions. It is settled: organized after the fall, coupled to it, the resting state of the record. Two weeks ago a shorter memory at 204 sessions had taken control; this week the deeper one took it back by strengthening (+0.03) while the challenger eased (−0.02). Both are coupled and lagging; nothing is pressing. The anti-coupled short end that was a watch last week faded. A strong fit, at the 83rd percentile for this memory length, in the most ordinary geometry the instrument has.

7 · The tells

Three ways from here

The board does not have a direction. It has two bodies, a long side that has started to tighten, and a Friday that has not reached the structural readers yet. Three branches, and the order in which the instrument will show which one it is.

Branch 1Two bodies, louder

The first mode keeps its split — same-sign share below 85% at 21 and 63 sessions — while it grows. The crest and trough hands stay half a cycle apart. The rooms hold. The long side keeps floating up through the floor without a new closure, or the trough cast closes next. Rotation, week four. The record's only precedent for a long split is the dot-com unwind — one case, survivorship-biased.

Branch 2One body

The 21-session same-sign share climbs back toward 95% while the first mode's share passes 30%; the whole market's count hand locks through 0.55; the crest and trough hands converge; the slow reader starts falling at the fast reader's pace, two points a week. February 2018 went from 83% / 11% to 99% / 33% in forty sessions. That is the path's shape, not its probability.

Branch 3The opposition fades

The 21-session first mode's share falls back under 22% as Thursday rolls deeper into the window; the fast reader recovers above the line; the frozen casts decohere (R below 0.5) rather than converge; the storm cast stays home. Thursday was one loud day inside a sorting that is losing its edge.

Outside the instrument · the analyst's layer

The board reads no news by design; this paragraph is the analyst's, kept separate. Facts before the close: Meta reported on October 21 — revenue $64.6B, up 26%; 2026 capital spending guided to $135–145B; a $9.9B legal charge — and the next day the ten largest lost 3.7% and the trough 115 2.2% at the median while 338 of 501 names rose. Reuters' Friday close: tech steadying after Thursday's AI selloff, oil at a six-month high on Middle East supply concern, the ten-year near 4.99%; the broad day with energy the exception. Interpretation: an AI-spending reassessment concentrated in the short side fits Thursday; oil-and-rates pressure fits Friday. Neither explains the structure — the two-sided first mode dates from July, three months before Meta's print, and the long side was below the floor before Friday. The comparison that would weaken the AI account: the trough cast rising through next week's prints while the crest keeps falling. Next watch, not an explanation of Friday: the Fed's statement Wednesday, October 28; Alphabet Tuesday after the close, Microsoft Wednesday, Amazon and Intel Thursday after the close — three of the ten companies inside the week the fast reader will carry Friday's common day. (Earnings dates from a third-party aggregator; unconfirmed.)

The instrument's words

A short glossary

The story count · degrees of freedom
The effective number of independent directions in the 500 stocks' standardized daily returns over a window (the participation ratio of the return covariance's eigenvalues). The fast reader uses 21 sessions, the slow reader 63. A crater is the slow reader falling under 55% of its trailing-year median.
The first mode · same-sign share
The single biggest shared direction in those returns, and the fraction of names on the same side of it. 99% is the market factor. 79% is a long-short factor with a fifth of the names on the short leg.
Freedom (inside a group)
The same participation ratio computed on one group's names, divided by the most it could be — the window length or the group's size. One: every name its own story. Near zero: a block.
The dial · phase · hand · R
Each stock's price against its own 20-session average gives a position in its swing: home (just rallied) at the top, the trough (just sold off) at the bottom, clockwise. A group's hand is its average position; R is how tightly it agrees (below 0.35: no position). A position says where a stock is in its recent swing, not where it goes next.
The crest 315 · the trough 115
The names the dial placed just past home and just past the trough on Tuesday, October 21, held fixed by name since. The long and short sides of the rotation. Nothing is re-sorted after the fact.
The ten
The ten largest cap lines in the index — nine companies, Alphabet twice — 39% of its value.
The floor · pressure · the float
The map's vertical axis: each stock's participation in the market's shared moves against its own normal. Below the white floor is above-normal. Pressure decays with a 21-session half-life unless a closure refills it; the float back up is arithmetic.
A closure · a release
A session on which at least 8% of the pool (51 of 648) crest together in their own swings. The ledger's newest tick prints low and its first revisions high; a count is a sketch for about a week.
Coupling · the crowd · dispersal
The map's horizontal axis: how tightly a stock's participation tracks the market's pulse. Tight and above-normal is the crowd; outside its own band and loosely tied is dispersal (the breakaway corner, Door B).
The river · rooms · matched-J
The board's clustering of the 500 by who moved in phase with whom over 63 sessions. Rooms are the clusters; matched-J is the day-to-day overlap of their membership.
The amplitude book · the spectrogram · an agreement day
How loud each stock's swing is against its own history, and whether the names agree about it, at memories from 21 to 756 sessions. Rust is agreement, blue disagreement. An agreement day is the spread across names falling under its own trailing-year floor. The newest column prints hot and settles.
The memory · settled
The lookback at which the market's participation energy and its drawdown are most organized (396 sessions now, correlation 0.90, energy lagging). Settled is the lagging, coupled geometry — organized after a fall; the record's resting state.
Then and now
Every stock's phase, loudness and closure flag is recomputed when a day is added, so yesterday as drawn today differs from yesterday as printed yesterday. The morning prints are kept; the redraws are labeled.

The story-count construction is the board's own (build_field_rank_c9.py: z-scored log returns, 90% finite columns, min 100 names, window excluding the labeled day), reproduced to 1e−14 before being decomposed.
  • The frozen casts are Sol's map_dial_named_endpoints.csv (selected from the dial's own October 21 print). Sol's measurements this edition relies on — the PR path and its fixed-roster check, the agreement-day counts and morning prints, the quiet-tail baselines, the storm-cast follow-up, the map's float decomposition, the river's rooms and matched-J, the Waves contest — are in comms/sol_20261025/ and credited where used.
  • Reference for every historical comparison: pool 650 / prices 49a5aa35 / endpoint 2026-10-23 / today's survivors back to 2000 (survivorship before 2015). Conditions in the crossing census and the tilt-run table were written after seeing Friday's shape; outcome windows overlap. An independent fact-check re-derived every number in this edition from the raw files with its own scripts (FACTCHECK.md); the census was restated from 47 to 46 complete windows after it (the 2000-10-20 crossing fell in the line's first weeks, before "since 2001").
